It probably was just a balance decision (making *all* the wraiths immune to
non-agg would make most wraiths too powerful). If you thought Ambrosius with a
Talbot's was bad, what if Brigitte, Felix, and even the Puppeteer could do the
same thing? Any deck without agg would be pretty much screwed. And you have a
bunch of blockers who can dish out damage and take none in return.

In addition, it could be circumstantial that all mummies return to your
library. Why do all mummies have 3 life? Why do all werewolves have 3 life? Why
do all mages have 0 strength and a ranged attack? Through comparisons and
analysis, you're trying to draw conclusions and connections that aren't
necessarily there. Why do the Renegade Garou and Black Spiral Buddy
"regenerate" while the Werewolf Pack doesn't? Or "Why is it that all mummies
return to your library when burnt but not all mages have manuevers like the
Outcast Mage, Thadius Zho, and Talaq the Immortal?" In addition, I'm sure it's
hypothetically possible that there might be a new Mummy card that *doesn't*
return to your library when built...

>Seems to imply to me that wraithes or the state of wraithness are
>ethereal and thus immune to non-agg.

In addition, let me emphasize that I'm no Wraith expert. Maybe there's an
in-game, logical explanation as to why some types of wraiths are immune while
other types aren't. Any wraith experts out there?

Halcyan 2

Funny, I have recently been reading up on Wraith: The Oblivion and
Mummy: The Ressurection (both of which you should buy, and no, I am not
affiliated with White Wolf ;) ).

Possible Wraith spoiling, if you haven't read Ends of Empire.

Although Ferrymen are Wraiths, they have a number of distinct advantages
over a normal Wraith, maybe the most important one being the lack of a
Shadow. When become a ferryman, they undergo a ritual which removes the
Shadow. It does have the nasty side effect of creating a separate creature
of immense power (essentially the shadow comes alive as a separate
creature equal in power to the Ferryman). This creature takes off to
create havoc elsewhere.

The Ferryman doesn't have to struggle with the Shadow on a day to day, and
I also believe they don't undergo Harrowings in the same way other Wraiths
do. Plus, to even be considered for a Ferryman, you have to be absurdley
powerful in the Arcanoi (the Wraithly disciplines).

Perhaps this is why Ambrosius has the non-agg damage benefit... to
represent just how damn tough Ferryman are. There may be
other reasons in the Wraithly world that I am not thinking of either.

There are a whole bunch of additional benefits for Ferryman, detailed in
Ends of the Empire. They also have some short comings, but they are few.

As for the mummies, they are pretty much indestructable (Bane mummy and
otherwise). They mention that there are a few ways for a Mummy to be
destroyed forever (they particularly mention some Cathayan powers which
will do so). But Mummy's all seem to return back from the Underworld,
without exception.

In short, I think the 'shuffling back into the deck' ability all the
mummies have is because ALL mummies return. The other allies have
differences to reflect their unique abilities. Hell, even the mummies have
unique powers. Not all of them have Amam's diablerie capability, for
example.

It's probably just to make the game interesting too. How boring would it
be if every mage had a maneuver, did 2R, bled at +1? Why bother creating
new allies?

"A Harrowing is a nightmare ride through the Tempest, a passion play or
psycho-drama starring the wraith and directed by the wraith's Shadow
with a supporting cast of Spectres. Harrowings are designed to torture
a wraith, empower her Shadow and force her into making mistakes which
may rip away her Passions, Fetters or her very essence and send her
screaming to Oblivion. To some extent, the Harrowing is like a game, a
challenge to the wraith to choose the right course of action which will
allow her to escape from the nightmare. Naturally, the Shadow tries
either to stack the cards so that the wraith chooses incorrectly, or to
make all choices seem so ill that the wraith cannot decide among them
and consequently does nothing. In either case, the Shadow 'wins' and
takes as its prize some part of the wraith's Passions or Fetters. This
weakens them and brings them closer to the nothingness of Oblivion - or
drags the wraith down into the Void. If the wraith triumphs, she breaks
free of the Harrowing and retains her Fetters and Passions. Though she
may be unscathed, she is usually not unchanged."

Wraith: The Oblivion, 2nd edition, page 183.

>So why dont they just go incorporeal in the first place?

Doesn't work like that. A wraith in the skin-lands is corporeal until
hit. (At which point they go incorporeal for several turns, based on
their stamina.)

There's probably an Arcanoi power that allows it too, though a brief
scan doesn't show any up in the basic book.

The Ash Path
**** Ex Nihilo

Ex Nihilo allows a necromancer to enter the Underworld physically.
While in the lands of the dead, the vampire is essentially an extra-
solid ghost. He maintains his normal number of health levels, but can
be hurt only by things that inflict aggravated damage on ghosts (weapons
forged from souls, certain ghostly powers etc.) A vampire physically in
the Underworld can pass through solid objects (at the cost of one health
level) and remain "incorporeal" thus for a number of turns equal to his
Stamina rating. On the other hand, vampires present in the Underworld
are subject to all of the Underworld's perils, including ultimate
destruction. A vampire killed in the Deadlands is gone forever, beyond
even the reach of other necromancers.

- Vampire: The Masquerade, 3rd edition, pp. 164-5

The card does quite a good job of mimicking such, whilst still leaving a
useful card at the end of it.
